title: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy (happily): "Mai, in summer you wear shorts and sandals. In winter you wear a big puffy coat. But why does the weather change at all?" Mai (surprised): "Wait, it does not just happen by magic?"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Here is a surprise. Earth comes closest to the Sun in early January. But January is winter in the top half of the world! Today we will find out what really makes summer, autumn, winter and spring."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Mai (proudly): "I know! In summer, Earth moves closer to the Sun. In winter, it moves far away." Huy (happily): "That is a great guess, Mai. Near a heater you feel warm, and far away you feel cooler. Lots of grown-ups think this too."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "But look at Earth's path around the Sun. It is almost a perfect circle, so the distance changes only a little. And Earth is closest in January, when the north is having winter!" Mai (surprised): "Closest, and it is still cold?"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Here is another clue. On the very same day, it can be winter in Canada and summer in Australia. If distance made the seasons, the whole Earth would have summer at once." Mai: "Then what makes them?" Huy (happily): "The secret is a tilt!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Step one. Earth travels around the Sun in a giant loop called an orbit. One full trip takes about 365 days. That is one year!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away. In one year, Earth travels about 940 million kilometres around it." Mai (laughing): "And I thought the walk to school was long!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Earth also spins, like a spinning top. It turns around an invisible line that goes through the North Pole and the South Pole. That line is called the axis. One spin gives us one day and one night."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Now here is the secret. Earth's axis is not straight up and down. It leans to one side, by about 23 degrees. We call that the tilt." Mai (laughing): "Earth is like me leaning back on my chair!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "And the tilt always points the same way in space, all year long, wherever Earth is in its orbit." Huy (firmly): "So remember. Earth is tilted, and the tilt always points the same way."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Step two. Let's watch Earth travel. In June, the top half of Earth leans toward the Sun."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Each half of Earth has a name. Half of a ball is called a hemisphere. The top half is the Northern Hemisphere. The bottom half is the Southern Hemisphere."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Six months later, in December, Earth is on the other side of the Sun. The tilt still points the same way. So now the north leans away from the Sun."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Mai (happily): "Let me try! I walk around the lamp, and keep my ball leaning toward the window. Now the top leans toward the lamp. Now it leans away!" Huy (proudly): "Exactly! For half the year, your half of Earth leans toward the Sun. For the other half, it leans away."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Step three. Why does leaning toward the Sun make it warm? First, the Sun climbs high in the sky. In winter, it stays low, even at lunchtime." Mai (surprised): "That is why my shadow is so long in winter!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "A high Sun shines straight down. Watch this torch. Point it straight down, and you get a small, bright spot."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Now tilt the torch, like a low winter Sun. The same light spreads over a much bigger patch, so each bit gets less." Mai (laughing): "It is like spreading a tiny bit of butter on a giant piece of toast!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Second, when your half leans toward the Sun, the days are longer. The Sun rises early and sets late, so the ground has more hours to warm up. In winter, days are short and nights are long."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "The longest day of the year is called the summer solstice. In the north, it comes around 21 June. The shortest day, the winter solstice, comes around 21 December. Solstice comes from old Latin words meaning the sun stands still."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "In between, around 20 March and 23 September, day and night are about the same length. These days are called equinoxes, and they mark spring and autumn." Mai (happily): "So spring and autumn are the in-between seasons!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "The hottest weeks usually come about a month after the longest day. The land and sea take time to warm up, just like a swimming pool stays chilly at the start of summer." Huy (firmly): "High Sun and long days make summer. Low Sun and short days make winter."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Step four. Because Earth is tilted, the two hemispheres always have opposite seasons. When the north leans away and has winter, the south leans toward the Sun and has summer."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Mai (surprised): "So kids in Australia have summer in December?" Huy (happily): "Yes! In Australia, summer begins on 1 December. Some kids build sandcastles while others are building snowmen!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Near the middle of the Earth, the temperature does not change very much. Many of these places have just two seasons, a rainy season and a dry season. The top part of Australia is like this."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Near the poles, the tilt makes things extreme. In summer, the Sun stays up even at midnight. That is the midnight sun. In winter, some days have no sunshine at all. That is polar night." Mai (surprised): "Bedtime in daylight? I would need very thick curtains!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Seasons change how we live too. Farmers often plant crops in spring and harvest them in autumn." Huy (firmly): "So the season you get depends on where on Earth you live."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Mai: "Huy, what if Earth stood up straight, with no tilt at all?" Huy: "Then the Sun's height and the length of the day would hardly change all year. Scientists think the seasons would almost disappear!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Some planets lean much more than Earth. Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side, tilted about 98 degrees! Scientists think a giant crash long ago may have knocked it over." Mai (laughing): "Poor Uranus, it fell over and never got up!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "You can check the torch trick at home with a grown-up. Shine a torch straight down on paper and draw around the bright spot. Then tilt the torch and draw again." Mai (proudly): "The tilted spot is bigger and dimmer, just like winter sunshine!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "So, why do we have seasons? Earth is tilted. As it travels around the Sun, each half leans toward the Sun and then away. Leaning toward means a high Sun and long days, so summer. Leaning away means winter."
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy: "Fun fact. Earth zooms around the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second. That is fast enough to cross the whole width of the Earth in about 7 minutes!" Mai (surprised): "And I cannot even feel it moving!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy

scenes.narration: Huy (happily): "Next time, we will ask why the sky is blue. Do not miss it!" Mai (joyfully): "Subscribe and come back with your own questions!"
scenes.chapter: Why Do We Have Seasons? | Ask Huy
